analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and insurers to publish the prices they negotiate, in plain language and free online.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Health Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any action after its introduction in March 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written hospital and insurer price-disclosure rules into federal law. Hospitals would have to publish, in plain language and a machine-readable format, their list prices, the rates they negotiated with each insurer, their cash-pay discounts, and billing codes for at least 300 common shoppable services [S3]. Health insurance plans, including employer plans, would have to publish their in-network and out-of-network rates and the net prices they actually pay for prescription drugs after rebates, and provide a free online tool where consumers can look up what a service will cost them [S2] [S3]. Hospitals that did not comply could face civil penalties of up to $300 per day [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone paying for health care. Today, hospitals and insurers negotiate rates in secret, and two people receiving the same service at the same hospital can be charged very different amounts. Under this bill, a consumer could look up what their insurer actually pays a hospital before scheduling care, compare cash prices against insurance prices, and see what their plan really pays for drugs after rebates — information that could let them shop for cheaper care and put pressure on hospitals and insurers to charge less.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and anyone paying for care

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals must publish, free and without a subscription, a list of standard charges including the rates negotiated with each named insurer, their highest and lowest negotiated rates, discounted cash prices, and billing codes [S2] [S3].

Hospitals must disclose this pricing for at least 300 common services that can be scheduled in advance, or maintain a free online price-estimator tool that gives consumers a real estimate of what they will owe [S3].
Insurance plans — including employer group plans, both self-insured and fully insured — must publish in-network and out-of-network rates and the negotiated prices for covered prescription drugs [S2].

Plans must provide a free internet-based tool that gives real-time, plain-language estimates of an individual's actual cost-sharing for a covered service, and consumers can request paper copies of the information [S2] [S3].

The drug price disclosure includes the 'historical net price' — what the insurer actually paid after rebates and discounts — which would expose the gap between a drug's list price and its real cost [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and health insurers, who would bear the cost of compiling and publishing their negotiated rates and building consumer-facing price tools. Hospitals that fail to comply face civil penalties capped at $300 per day — a small sum for most hospital systems. Insurers and pharmacy middlemen would also face pressure on prices once their negotiated rates and drug rebate amounts become public, since consumers and employers could use the data to negotiate lower rates.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement penalty is capped at $300 per day for a hospital out of compliance, which is small relative to hospital revenues and may not be enough to force compliance [S3].

Compliance costs fall on hospitals and insurers, who must reorganize and publish large amounts of contracting data and maintain consumer tools — costs that could partly be passed back through premiums and charges.

Full rate transparency can cut both ways: making the highest negotiated rates public can give low-priced hospitals and providers leverage to push their rates up toward the top, potentially raising some prices rather than lowering them.

Similar hospital and insurer transparency rules already exist through federal regulation from the prior administration, so the bill's practical effect would have been to lock those rules into statute rather than create them fresh — meaningful for durability, less so for immediate change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit to consumers is real but modest: it largely turns existing regulatory transparency requirements into statute, making them harder for a future administration to weaken, and adds detail like drug net prices after rebates. The cost is compliance work for hospitals and insurers and a possible upward drift in some low negotiated rates. Its biggest weakness is its own design — a $300-per-day penalty cap gives large hospital systems little reason to fear noncompliance. On balance, the disclosure requirements would have given ordinary patients significantly more price information at little direct cost to them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2023 and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never considered it; it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Braun introduced the bill on March 30, 2023, joined by Senator Chuck Grassley as its only cosponsor [S1] [S4].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers came out ahead: no law required them to publish their negotiated rates, so contracting data stayed private and rate transparency remained dependent on regulations that a future administration could loosen. Patients gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and insurers who avoided a disclosure law

for.name: Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put forward statutory hospital and insurer price-disclosure requirements.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it had no other cosponsors in either party.

against.name: Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing, markup, or vote during the two-year Congress, so it never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republican senators backed the bill and no Democrat cosponsored it, and the Democrat-led committee it was referred to never gave it any action before Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill would have forced hospitals to publish their negotiated rates with each insurer, cash prices, and billing codes for 300 common services, exposing the wide variation in what different patients pay for the same care. Hospitals had kept this data secret; the bill's penalty cap of $300 per day limited how painful compliance could be.

Plans, including self-insured employer plans, would have had to publish in-network and out-of-network rates and build free real-time cost-estimator tools for members. Public disclosure of negotiated rates would let consumers and employers shop plans and negotiate rates down.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and the drug rebate chain
industries.note: The bill required insurers to disclose the 'historical net price' of drugs — what they actually paid after rebates and discounts — and defined negotiated rates to include amounts paid indirectly through pharmacy benefit managers. This would have exposed how much of a drug's list price is absorbed by rebates and middlemen.
